item.title: A few Zigbee sensors and a light switch replaced my $250 Ring alarm system
item.itunes:title: A few Zigbee sensors and a light switch replaced my $250 Ring alarm system
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We've had someone pop round to provide a quote for a monitored alarm system, and it's quite something. I don't want to pay much and don't really feel the need to have it monitored since I could contact the authorities myself and have them attend the scene. Plus, I've already configured the property with strategically positioned cameras, so I thought I'd build a smart home alarm system myself, using nothing but some Zigbee sensors, a screen, and one light switch housing. The result is a clean, subscription-free, and versatile security solution.

Saving money on the hardware

Do you really need live monitoring?

A Ring alarm starter kit costs around $250 for the base station, a keypad, four door/window sensors, an extender, and a single motion sensor. A pack of four Zgibee door sensors can be bought for $40. A single motion sensor is around $16. That's $56 so far. Sonoff sells an excellent NSPanel display and light switch for $129, which can then all be linked together with a Zigbee broadcaster for Home Assistant on a separate server. Without factoring in that cost, it's $185 for a similar DIY alarm setup.

Except, unlike Ring products, everything here is powered by Zigbee, and I can customize it how I see fit, use third-party integrations, and configure automations to personalize the alarm system to our needs. The four-door sensors take care of the side entrance, main entrance, rear doors, and office door. The hallway is fairly tight, so that single motion sensor is perfect for keeping tabs on movement throughout the house. The NSPanel Pro can be used as the brain of the operation, but here it's tasked with boosting the Zigbee signal and interacting with Home Assistant.

Zigbee is great for these low-powered devices, as it means they don't need to use too much battery. The two AAA modules inside each door sensor should last for months, if not years, depending on usage and how many times the doors are opened and closed. To control everything is my Sonoff 3.0 Zigbee dongle connected directly to the Proxmox server running Home Assistant. This configuration is neat, keeps as much off Wi-Fi as possible, and is pretty much completely open, allowing me to fully customize it.

Something I didn't mention yet is there's not a single subscription here. We paid for Ring Premium since we had a doorbell and the alarm system, which allowed it to be monitored. This wasn't particularly useful. We'd get a call most times (not all), and Ring can't actually notify the authorities. For that to happen, the system needs to be professionally installed and monitored. It just didn't feel like the alarm system was nearby. So, now we can have an almost identical setup without spending a penny each month.

Stop automating your schedule — use a cheap sensor to automate your actions instead

Your home should work for you.

1
By  Jasmine Mannan

Installing your own alarm system is easy

Everything using the same dedicated network

I already planned out how everything was going to be positioned. The issue with the existing home alarm system we had with Ring was it required three power outlets. One for the primary hub, another for the extender, and a third for the keypad. You'd need four if using the doorbell and chime. This new Zigbee setup would require none ... or rather one when counting the Proxmox server. But since we already had Proxmox and Home Assistant running, it's almost for free.

The existing keypad was awkwardly positioned in the hallway above a single power outlet. This needed to be disconnected each time we required access to the outlet, so I opted to move to a powered screen, the NSPanel Pro Gen2 from Sonoff. It's powered by Android, can connect to and launch with Home Assistant, and takes five minutes to install. All I required was a free single light switch that could be removed. The NSPanel doubles as a smart display and relay for two light fixtures.

The metal light box I selected was a little tight, however, and so I opted for a 10mm spacer bracket, costing $4. After installing the screen, the result was a flush, sleek-looking alarm panel that doubled up as a smart home display. We could view energy cards, have access to Alarmo, and toggle the light switch as usual. Not a single cable needed to be routed. The panel has a speaker, and if we wanted, we could always pick up a dedicated Zigbee alarm siren and still be under the cost of a Ring kit.

I finally set up Home Assistant with Zigbee, and my entire home changed

I had heard about Zigbee for a long time, but I finally took the plunge. I should have sooner.

12
By  Adam Conway

Using Alarmo in Home Assistant

It's a match made in heaven

Alarmo is an available Home Assistant integration, which essentially functions as a home security control center. It takes sensor inputs from all our Zigbee devices, including an existing water leak sensor, and provides the means to configure various modes, codes, and more. And because it's all heavily customizable, I could configure each mode setting to perform actions, such as sending notifications to devices and playing audio files. Now, we have mobile notifications for doors and audible announcements.

Ring's own settings were limited, and a chime didn't really notify precisely what was going on. If I didn't have my phone with me to spot the back door opening, I'd be none the wiser. And remember those cameras connected through Frigate? I can set automations to task Frigate with snapshotting and saving clips if an alarm triggers. I can use object detection to work out what could have triggered an alarm if in view. Camera feeds can be passed through to the NSPanel so everyone in the home can see what's outside.

If an alarm sounds, I can check the feeds and see a quick history snapshot of what happened just before it was triggered. The alarm can then be disabled if it's a false alarm, or I can notify authorities immediately. If I want, I can add other branded hardware further down the line, opening up new avenues for perfecting our smart home and securing it. But most of all, everything stays online without a reliance on third-party services.

It's not for everyone, however

That said, though I thoroughly enjoyed creating this setup and I'm happy with the results, it's not perfect. First, like other DIY solutions, there isn't any live monitoring. I need to be the point of contact for authorities. Second, it's not suitable for insurance or legally required systems. Our home insurance provider won't care how many sensors and sirens I have installed. But to save some money while still offering good levels of protection? It's not too bad at all!

item.title: I replaced Windows' app updater with one tool that actually lets me manage all my apps
item.itunes:title: I replaced Windows' app updater with one tool that actually lets me manage all my apps
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a long time, Windows lacked basic package management capabilities, but that changed in recent years with the introduction of the aptly-named Windows Package Manager (also called winget). The problem with this tool, however, is that it's just that: a fairly basic package manager that may not cover all your needs.

Thankfully, there's a better solution in the form of UniGetUI. This tool isn't just one package manager, it's all of them, meaning it makes it easier than ever to manage and update all my Windows 11 apps in one place. And it has other perks, too.

UniGetUI has come a long way

It's not a small project anymore

I want to provide some context for UniGetUI, because it's not often that you get to follow a project from so early on in its life and see it come this far. This project started many years ago as WingetUI, and it was just meant to provide a graphical interface for Winget, but it later evolved into UniGetUI, and I even wrote about it two years ago when it was still relatively early on in its development.

UniGetUI was a completely independent project, but earlier this year, it was acquired by Devolutions, which has vowed to keep the app free while giving it much more reliable backing and support. That's a common fear with projects started by a single person, so this acquisition may actually be a good one.

5 Reasons UniGetUI is the best package manager for Windows

If you want the easiest way to install you favorite apps and utilities, UniGetUI is the best package manager you can use.

3
By  Brian Burgess

When the buyout was announced, Devolutions said UniGetUI has 300,000 monthly active users, which is a positive surprise to see for a project that seemed relatively small in scale just a couple of years ago. There are even versions of the tool for macOS and Linux now, which is wild to see for what seemed like such a Windows-centric project.

It updates and installs (almost) all my apps

Winget is just a piece of the puzzle

UniGetUI brings together all major package managers for Windows, including Winget, Chocolatey, and Scoop, but also includes more dedicated packages, like items from the PowerShell Gallery, .NET packages, and Npm. Almost everything you can think of can be updated through UniGetUI.

While Winget does have the majority of apps you'd want, there are clear benefits to having more package managers here. For one thing, things like PowerShell Gallery and Npm are important for specific kinds of users and there's no way to easily manage these tools through Winget.

But even for Chocolatey and Scoop, which are conceptually closer to Winget, you may prefer using those over Microsoft's own app updater. Some developers may also choose to avoid Microsoft's repository, meaning some important apps may only be on these other package managers. It's important to have choice.

Chocolatey vs. Winget vs. Scoop: Battle of the Windows package managers

Over the years, the Windows ecosystem has seen the emergence of some cool package managers. But which one comes out on top?

5
By  Ayush Pande

UniGetUI gives you all of these sources in one place, which isn't just convenient because you have a centralized place to do it, but it also presents it to you in a more human-readable format, since it's a proper GUI. You can easily select updates to install or skip, see version numbers, and so on.

On top of that, it's automated. UniGetUI can check for updates on your behalf and let you know what's available so you can update as soon as possible. It takes a lot of work out of keeping your PC secure and up to date. However, you're still in control. when you first install an app through UniGetUI, you can choose to enable or disable automatic updates, or just freeze it out of updates entirely in the future.

Bundles make it easier to set up a new PC

Install your apps in one go

Bringing multiple sources of apps and packages together is already a huge advantage, but what takes UniGetUi that much further is its concept of app bundles, which you can create and save for yourself, or share as needed.

Bundles let you group together multiple packages from across any source of your choosing. These groups of apps can then be loaded on a system so you can install them all in one go, or select the ones you need the most. Say you're in an enterprise environment or school where multiple PCs all have the same apps. You can create a bundle with these apps, store it in a shared location, and load it up in UniGetUI to install all those apps in one go.

When I first tested UniGetUI a few years ago, this feature was at least partly broken, but now, it works perfectly. I was able to install the same set of apps on two of my laptops with no issues, and it was far easier than it would have been otherwise. The current version of the app also lets you create a PowerShell script for installing the apps, rather than forcing you to install them all using UniGetUI again. It's great to see how far it's come.

7 ways package managers make your life easier on Windows 11

Package managers like Chocolatey simplify installs, updates, and removals on Windows, saving time, reducing bloat, and enhancing security.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

To be clear, Winget also lets you back up installed apps and restore them in one go, but you have very little control over it. It backs up all the packages you've installed through Winget (except the ones that fail), and it installs the apps in the backup unless you modify that backup file. UniGetUI is just far more flexible, on top of supporting apps form multiple sources.

It's not all automatic

You do need to do some work yourself

The downside to all the capabilities of UniGetUI is that not all of it will be ready to go by default. UniGetUI will detect the installations of the tools you already have, so things like Winget will work out of the box, but for Chocolatey, Scoop, Npm, Pip, and others, you need to install the respective package managers.

That may make UniGetUI feel a bit redundant, since you still need to set up a few things beforehand, but it does make things a lot easier to have all these package managers in one place, even if they're still installed individually. It also gives you the freedom to interact with them on your terms at any given time. Maybe you want to use a GUI occasionally, but also have the terminal available. You always have that option.

UniGetUI is the be-all and end-all of package managers

By bringing together so many package managers in one place, including search and update management, automating the update process, and allowing you to create custom bundles of apps, UniGetUI is an essential tool for managing your apps on Windows 11. If you truly care about keeping your software up to date, I can't recommend it enough.

item.content:encoded:
For a long time, Windows lacked basic package management capabilities, but that changed in recent years with the introduction of the aptly-named Windows Package Manager (also called winget). The problem with this tool, however, is that it's just that: a fairly basic package manager that may not cover all your needs.

Thankfully, there's a better solution in the form of UniGetUI. This tool isn't just one package manager, it's all of them, meaning it makes it easier than ever to manage and update all my Windows 11 apps in one place. And it has other perks, too.

UniGetUI has come a long way

It's not a small project anymore

I want to provide some context for UniGetUI, because it's not often that you get to follow a project from so early on in its life and see it come this far. This project started many years ago as WingetUI, and it was just meant to provide a graphical interface for Winget, but it later evolved into UniGetUI, and I even wrote about it two years ago when it was still relatively early on in its development.

UniGetUI was a completely independent project, but earlier this year, it was acquired by Devolutions, which has vowed to keep the app free while giving it much more reliable backing and support. That's a common fear with projects started by a single person, so this acquisition may actually be a good one.

5 Reasons UniGetUI is the best package manager for Windows

If you want the easiest way to install you favorite apps and utilities, UniGetUI is the best package manager you can use.

3
By  Brian Burgess

When the buyout was announced, Devolutions said UniGetUI has 300,000 monthly active users, which is a positive surprise to see for a project that seemed relatively small in scale just a couple of years ago. There are even versions of the tool for macOS and Linux now, which is wild to see for what seemed like such a Windows-centric project.

It updates and installs (almost) all my apps

Winget is just a piece of the puzzle

UniGetUI brings together all major package managers for Windows, including Winget, Chocolatey, and Scoop, but also includes more dedicated packages, like items from the PowerShell Gallery, .NET packages, and Npm. Almost everything you can think of can be updated through UniGetUI.

While Winget does have the majority of apps you'd want, there are clear benefits to having more package managers here. For one thing, things like PowerShell Gallery and Npm are important for specific kinds of users and there's no way to easily manage these tools through Winget.

But even for Chocolatey and Scoop, which are conceptually closer to Winget, you may prefer using those over Microsoft's own app updater. Some developers may also choose to avoid Microsoft's repository, meaning some important apps may only be on these other package managers. It's important to have choice.

Chocolatey vs. Winget vs. Scoop: Battle of the Windows package managers

Over the years, the Windows ecosystem has seen the emergence of some cool package managers. But which one comes out on top?

5
By  Ayush Pande

UniGetUI gives you all of these sources in one place, which isn't just convenient because you have a centralized place to do it, but it also presents it to you in a more human-readable format, since it's a proper GUI. You can easily select updates to install or skip, see version numbers, and so on.

On top of that, it's automated. UniGetUI can check for updates on your behalf and let you know what's available so you can update as soon as possible. It takes a lot of work out of keeping your PC secure and up to date. However, you're still in control. when you first install an app through UniGetUI, you can choose to enable or disable automatic updates, or just freeze it out of updates entirely in the future.

Bundles make it easier to set up a new PC

Install your apps in one go

Bringing multiple sources of apps and packages together is already a huge advantage, but what takes UniGetUi that much further is its concept of app bundles, which you can create and save for yourself, or share as needed.

Bundles let you group together multiple packages from across any source of your choosing. These groups of apps can then be loaded on a system so you can install them all in one go, or select the ones you need the most. Say you're in an enterprise environment or school where multiple PCs all have the same apps. You can create a bundle with these apps, store it in a shared location, and load it up in UniGetUI to install all those apps in one go.

When I first tested UniGetUI a few years ago, this feature was at least partly broken, but now, it works perfectly. I was able to install the same set of apps on two of my laptops with no issues, and it was far easier than it would have been otherwise. The current version of the app also lets you create a PowerShell script for installing the apps, rather than forcing you to install them all using UniGetUI again. It's great to see how far it's come.

7 ways package managers make your life easier on Windows 11

Package managers like Chocolatey simplify installs, updates, and removals on Windows, saving time, reducing bloat, and enhancing security.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

To be clear, Winget also lets you back up installed apps and restore them in one go, but you have very little control over it. It backs up all the packages you've installed through Winget (except the ones that fail), and it installs the apps in the backup unless you modify that backup file. UniGetUI is just far more flexible, on top of supporting apps form multiple sources.

It's not all automatic

You do need to do some work yourself

The downside to all the capabilities of UniGetUI is that not all of it will be ready to go by default. UniGetUI will detect the installations of the tools you already have, so things like Winget will work out of the box, but for Chocolatey, Scoop, Npm, Pip, and others, you need to install the respective package managers.

That may make UniGetUI feel a bit redundant, since you still need to set up a few things beforehand, but it does make things a lot easier to have all these package managers in one place, even if they're still installed individually. It also gives you the freedom to interact with them on your terms at any given time. Maybe you want to use a GUI occasionally, but also have the terminal available. You always have that option.

UniGetUI is the be-all and end-all of package managers

By bringing together so many package managers in one place, including search and update management, automating the update process, and allowing you to create custom bundles of apps, UniGetUI is an essential tool for managing your apps on Windows 11. If you truly care about keeping your software up to date, I can't recommend it enough.

item.title: Valve's new Remote Play codec uses up to 10 times more bandwidth on purpose, and it's the first time streaming has felt like sitting at the PC
item.itunes:title: Valve's new Remote Play codec uses up to 10 times more bandwidth on purpose, and it's the first time streaming has felt like sitting at the PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Valve's new Pyrowave codec for Steam Remote Play sounds like excess for the sake of it on paper. Valve says it uses five to ten times the bandwidth of other streaming codecs, and in my testing Steam's overlay showed roughly 400 to 480 Mbit/s of video with full HDR and 4:4:4 color enabled. Nearly every video codec exists to shrink that bandwidth instead of grow it, but Pyrowave spends bandwidth to save time and latency instead, and on a wired home network where bandwidth is the one thing you have plenty of, that's a great trade.

I finally set up Steam Link for my TV, and now stream couch gaming from the other side of the house

Steam Link helped bring the joy back into PC gaming

By  Tanveer Singh

Why Pyrowave skips the compression trickery of other codecs

Sacrificing efficiency for speed

Codecs like H.264, HEVC, and AV1, which Remote Play already supports, get small streams largely by predicting what changes between frames and then squeezing the result with entropy coding. It's extremely efficient, but it takes time. Pyrowave, created by Hans-Kristian Arntzen, skips both. Its documentation describes it as, practically speaking, a still-image codec. Every frame is compressed on its own with no motion prediction. This is what drives a large increase in bitrate but it's easy work to parallelize on a GPU, so the performance hit is negligible.

It runs as Vulkan compute shaders on the GPU, and Arntzen lists encode and decode times under roughly 0.1 ms at 1080p and 0.2 ms at 4K. Valve describes total latency as encode plus network plus decode plus display, which is why it warns that your setup may not benefit.

I use this open-source tool to easily cast any video to my smart TV

Go2TV beats Plex for one thing: casting local videos without the library overhead

By  Dhruv Bhutani

What is looked like on my setup

Both a wired and wireless connection was really solid

The host was my Windows desktop, wired, with two very different clients. The first was a Minisforum MS-03 running Ubuntu 26.04 over Ethernet. In Escape From Tarkov at 4K and 120 fps, Steam's overlay reported under 1 ms of ping and 8.38 ms of display latency, with no packet or frame loss. In Battlefield 6, the capture ran near 97 fps and display latency rose to 13.64 ms. With the bandwidth limits set to unlimited, the visual fidelity was indistinguishable from the host experience.

Both games are relatively fast-paced shooters where input latency is really crucial, and I was pleasantly surprised by the performance. I could definitely tell that the game was being streamed, but it was by no means unplayable.

There was one small issue on the Linux box: my mouse input was quite stuttery and inconsistent, but this likely has something to do with the mouse itself or the way Linux handles the input. It's a mouse with a polling rate of 8K, so that combined with the potential inconsistency of how the input is being passed could've caused this but I couldn't nail it down. The other scenario I tested did not have this issue with a different input device.

The second client was an ASUS Zenbook on Wi-Fi 7 over the 5GHz band, right next to the access point, streaming 1080p at 120 fps. Its numbers were less flattering: 4.23 ms of ping but 30.06 ms of display latency. It still felt smooth in Tarkov, which was a pleasant surprise. I ran everything with 4:4:4 color on. Valve leaves it off by default because it needs more bandwidth and processing time, so your numbers may differ, but I wanted to see what the worst-case-scenario would be for bandwidth.

If I move around the house or didn't have a solid 5GHz connection, the experience really suffered, and that's shown by the latency graph's huge jump in the image above.

Moonlight and Apollo help me experience my PC games the console way

My PlayStation is shaking in terror

By  Samarveer Singh

Where Pyrowave falls short

The obvious catch is bandwidth

Steam lets you set a manual bitrate between 100 and 500 Mbit/s, and Valve recommends connecting both machines directly to your router over at least gigabit Ethernet. Arntzen himself says streaming over the internet isn't feasible at these rates outside peer-to-peer fiber links. Pyrowave also isn't a more efficient codec, only a faster one. Valve warns it may not lower latency on every setup, since the network and display still add delay, and the gap between my two clients shows the rest of the connection chain matters.

Linux gaming is getting faster because Windows APIs are becoming Linux kernel features

As time goes on, fewer games than ever are unplayable on Linux

18
By  Ty Sherback

Try it for yourself

The Steam Client beta has everything you need to try Pyrowave

To try out the new high-bandwidth codec with Remote Play, simply opt-in to the Steam Client beta. Next, open Remote Play's advanced client options on the client and enable Pyrowave before you start streaming. On Linux, turn on the experimental SteamRT3 client in Steam's system settings first. Automatic bitrate is the default, and you can switch to a manual setting between 100 and 500 Mbit/s if your network needs it. The 4:4:4 option is worth trying if you're streaming a desktop or reading text on a 4K display.

Steam Cloud hit its limit, so I built a better sync system with my home server and two free tools

Steam Cloud is great, but its limits pushed me to set up something even better

By  Ty Sherback

Steam Remote Play gets another codec option

Game streaming has always been a compromise: you squeeze the picture small enough to fit the network and accept the delay that squeezing adds. Valve's new Pyrowave codec for Steam Remote Play helps one side of that equation, but heavily inflates the other. Whether that's worth it to you is entirely dependent on your network scenario.

item.title: Gemini is getting rid of Gems, and its replacement aims to make repetitive work a lot easier
item.itunes:title: Gemini is getting rid of Gems, and its replacement aims to make repetitive work a lot easier
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Gemini replaces Gems with "skills" and migrates your existing Gems automatically.
  • Skills can be invoked with / (soon @), stacked in chats, and auto-invoke when useful.
  • Build a skill once to speed repetitive tasks: slides, matching your writing, or fresh viewpoints.

AI is really good at performing the same task over and over. If you ever find yourself feeding the same input to your LLM multiple times with only one thing that really changes, there are usually features that speed up the process and save all that copy-pasting. Google Gemini had Gems, but it's now being replaced by something simply called "skills."

Gemini skills help speed up the monotony of repetitive tasks

Set it up once, and you're done

As announced in News from Google, Gemini is transitioning away from the Gems system, replacing it with a very similar alternative called 'skills'. By the looks of it, there's not much that's vastly different between the old Gems system and Gemini skills, with Google providing the following examples of use:

  • Prepare for presentations: Build a custom skill to outline slides, craft talking points, and prep for tough Q&As, whether for a class presentation or a project pitch.
  • Match your writing style: Gemini knows your unique writing style across Workspace apps to speed up drafting, all while keeping you in full control.
  • Get more perspectives: Ask Gemini to always provide three to five distinct viewpoints on a topic to help you brainstorm ideas, refine arguments, or commit to a decision.

In fact, the systems are so similar that Google will simply move all of your existing Gems over to the skills system as it goes live today.

So, why is Google even bothering with this swap? Well, while the new skills system shares a lot of similarities with Gems, there are some key differences under the hood that make it even more useful. In a document about the transition from Gems to skills, Google explains that you can invoke a skill using a / (which will soon become a @), and you can stack multiple skills in a single chat. Plus, Gemini can automatically detect when a skill can come into use and invoke it when needed.

I tried Gemini, ChatGPT, and Copilot for a month and I have a clear winner for you

Don’t buy the hype.

12
By  Parth Shah

item.title: This one community Home Assistant integration saves me hundreds each year
item.itunes:title: This one community Home Assistant integration saves me hundreds each year
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Home Assistant is the backbone of our household. It's what allows us to enjoy smart technology that makes a difference. We're using it for our home alarm system, effectively replacing Ring, as well as controlling smart plugs and monitoring energy consumption. That's all well and good, but we even took it a step further with full power management automation, overseeing our home battery setup and controlling it to make the most of our solar production and save hundreds each year.

What we used to pay for electricity

It's not cheap running a home lab!

Our home is all electric. That's a blessing when it comes to renewables, but it can also be fairly alarming and means we pull a lot from the grid. An average day sees about 30 kWh pulled by the house. If we're also charging an EV overnight, this jumps to almost 50 kWh. That's a lot of power. Our electricity bill for the month of November 2025 alone was just shy of $700, thanks to a month-long cold spell, work being done around the house, and a few serious draughts.

Having just moved in, this was eye-watering, leading my spouse to immediately begin searching for solar energy to help offset the monthly utility bill. We managed to get a setup configured and commissioned in record time, allowing for savings to be enjoyed almost immediately, but I found the app lacking. It's not the worst around, but I find these software solutions with PV systems to be anything but feature-rich. AI is also making the rounds.

It's not terrible and does learn habits, use data for forecasting (I believe it does anyway), and adjust battery charge and discharge on the fly, but I found a better way to manage everything, and that was through Home Assistant. This way, I could see what inputs the system was taking to adjust things, and I could tailor it to our exact requirements.

5 useful Home Assistant automations I wish I had in my life sooner

From energy tracking to turning off devices when not in use, Home Assistant helps improve my life by automating my smart home.

item.itunes:title: I enabled this hidden Samsung setting and my Galaxy feels like a new phone
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My Galaxy S25 Ultra has never felt slow, but after using it every day for months, the interface had started to feel a little too familiar. App launches, swipe-up gestures, and transitions all worked fine, yet I couldn’t shake the feeling that One UI could feel quicker and more responsive.

I didn’t want to disable animations entirely or mess around with aggressive Developer Options tweaks just to save a few seconds. As it turns out, Samsung already gives me excellent control over all of this, but it hides those controls inside Good Lock’s Home Up module.

One UI is quietly killing your Samsung battery — here's which 6 settings to disable

Find out which unexpected OneUI features are secretly draining your Galaxy phone's battery and how to disable them.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

My Galaxy wasn’t slow, but it felt familiar

The speed wasn’t up to the Pixel and iPhone level

My Galaxy S25 Ultra was never actually slow. Apps opened quickly, multitasking was smooth, and I rarely ran into any real performance issues. But after comparing it with my iPhone 17 running iOS 27 and Pixel 8 running Android 17-based Pixel UI, One UI started to feel a little different in comparison.

The app-opening and home animations on my Galaxy felt slower and slightly rubbery, especially when I quickly swiped between apps or returned to the home screen. The phone had plenty of power, but the animations made it feel less immediate than the other two.

I could have opened Device Care, cleared memory, or used one of Samsung’s temporary performance-boosting options, but that wasn’t what I wanted. RAM wasn’t the problem, and I didn’t want a short-lived fix that I would have to repeat afterward.

I wanted something that permanently changed how One UI responded to my gestures. That’s when I started digging through Good Lock and found a neat option to boost my Galaxy S25 Ultra’s behavior.

Samsung hides much deeper animation controls

I changed how gestures respond

Samsung already gives me far more control over animations than I expected, but most of it is buried inside Good Lock. I opened Good Lock, downloaded the Home Up module, and headed to Gesture settings. From there, I enabled Home gesture animation tuning, which immediately opened up a few different animation styles.

The biggest change for me was switching from Classic to Dynamic. Dynamic makes the home gesture feel quicker and more responsive, without removing the animation entirely. It still looks polished, but there is less of that slow, rubbery movement I noticed before.

There is also a Simple tuning option with a slider, so I can fine-tune the animation instead of choosing a preset and calling it a day.

I also enabled App open animation tuning and moved the speed meter to Fast. That made an equally noticeable difference when launching apps. There is an Advanced tuning section too, with plenty of additional controls if I want to obsess over every detail, but I honestly didn’t need to go that far. These two changes were enough for me.

My Galaxy S25 Ultra now feels quicker. Apps seem to fly open, and swiping back to the home screen feels far more immediate. The hardware hasn’t changed, but the way One UI moves finally matches the speed I expect from a flagship phone.

It works better than the Developer Options trick

It makes One UI feel personalized

I have used the old Developer Options trick before, where I reduced the Window animation scale, Transition animation scale, and Animator duration scale to 0.5x. It makes Android feel faster, but it is also a pretty blunt solution.

Everything simply speeds up, whether the animation actually looks better or not. Good Lock feels much more refined. With Home Up, I am not just cutting animation time in half. I can change the animation style, adjust how quickly it reacts, and tune app-opening behavior. That gives me a much better balance between speed and polish.

I still get smooth transitions, but they no longer feel overly stretched out. This tweak also reminded me why Good Lock is one of my favorite parts of using a Samsung phone. I can change how gestures behave, how apps open, how the home screen works and looks, and even tweak the Samsung Keyboard.

That is why I would encourage Galaxy users to get a little creative with it instead of copying my exact settings. Home Up alone gives you plenty to experiment with, and the rest of Good Lock opens up even more possibilities.

My Samsung phone kept draining battery overnight, so I built this routine

My Galaxy finally sleeps properly now.

1
By  Parth Shah

The easiest Galaxy upgrade costs nothing

I didn’t expect an animation tweak to make such a noticeable difference, especially on a phone that was already fast to begin with. But that’s exactly why this setting surprised me.

This tweak changes the part of the experience I interact with constantly. After changing the animation behavior to my liking, the phone feels responsive and polished.

That’s the kind of customization I appreciate most about Samsung. Good Lock doesn’t just let me change how my Galaxy looks; it lets me change how it feels to use every day.

item.title: I calculated my old PC's true power cost as a home server, and it beat every alternative I tested
item.itunes:title: I calculated my old PC's true power cost as a home server, and it beat every alternative I tested
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Over the past year, my homelab has grown to include several machines, each with a specific job. An 8-year-old business laptop as an always-on home server, an old NAS for bulk storage, and a pretty powerful workstation for day-to-day tasks. I also have a MacBook that I mostly use while traveling.

I have been thinking about upgrading the server for a long time, since an old laptop running 24/7 looked like the first piece of hardware to replace with something better and more efficient. But nothing inspired me to get it right away. That was when, out of curiosity, I decided to calculate how much my setup was actually costing me to run.

I measured what my homelab actually consumes

The number I expected wasn't on the watts

I have been using an old business laptop as my home server for more than a year now. I never bought it. I got it from my relative, who was upgrading his Dell Latitude 7480 to a brand-new Surface Pro. So, technically, the old laptop was meant to be recycled, but instead I repurposed it as a bare-metal Debian server.

The Latitude runs on an Intel Core i5-6300U CPU, paired with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB of SSD. Obviously, 256 GB for a homelab with Jellyfin, Immich, and Nextcloud wasn’t enough, so I stripped my old Synology DS218J NAS to only one job and used it as bulk storage for the server.

For the last year, these two machines have been my whole homelab fleet: a handed-over business PC and an old NAS. You might think running a consumer-grade PC and an old NAS would consume a lot of power since they are always plugged into the wall, but the numbers show the opposite. I tested both the machines using a cheap smart plug from TP-Link.

When the server is idle, and by "idle" I mean running its normal services, containers, networking, etc., it usually sits around 10–15 watts. And when I push it to a larger load, like running multiple streams on Jellyfin, direct play and transcoding included, where the CPU pushes to more than 70% of its capacity, it roughly takes around 20–30 watts. And it’s a similar case for the NAS, roughly 10-15 watts.

Since both machines are part of a 24-hour running home server, they are both always powered on. So, if I do a little math and factor in idle and active time (22.5 hrs idle / 1.5 hrs active daily) from my monitoring tool Beszel, the monthly total consumption comes to around 10kWh for each.

I am not quoting the exact $ amount, as the numbers depend on where you live, but if I take the EIA's 2026 national average (18¢/kWh), it comes to around $3.5-4 every month. But the bill wasn’t a major concern for me; it was whether newer and more efficient setups could replace my current setup, and whether the additional cost would justify the power savings.

item.title: I made Android Auto render at a higher resolution in developer settings, and my car's screen finally looks sharp
item.itunes:title: I made Android Auto render at a higher resolution in developer settings, and my car's screen finally looks sharp
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My car didn't ship with Android Auto support, so I use an aftermarket infotainment system. This means Android Auto generally works fine in my car, but one annoying problem has been plaguing me.

The screen has never looked as sharp as I think it should. This is most noticeable around things like Google Maps and Waze, where the icons and text look softer than expected. In fact, anything with fine details tends to look upscaled. That shouldn't happen on a modern, high-end head unit with a tack-sharp HD display.

It turns out, the problem was simple. My phone wasn't negotiating the resolution correctly with the display, and all it took to fix it was changing the video resolution deep within Android Auto's developer options. That one setting made Android Auto look much cleaner on the same setup, without any hardware changes.

Android Auto doesn't always use the correct resolution

How to force Android Auto to use a higher resolution

Credit: 

Here's the problem. Android Auto doesn't simply mirror whatever is on your phone. The phone renders the Android Auto interface and sends a video stream to my car's head unit. That part is straightforward enough. But before that, the phone and head unit negotiate the resolution they will use. Android Auto supports everything from a low-res 800x480 pixel stream to a Full HD 1920x1080 video stream.

In theory, that negotiation should detect the infotainment system's display resolution and pass it to Android Auto. However, in practice, it doesn't always work like that consistently, especially if you're using a third-party Android Auto head unit. And when the resolution negotiation doesn't happen as expected, you can get streams that look soft, especially on higher-resolution car screens.

That's where the developer options come in. Most people never need to interact with the Android Auto settings on their phone. The entire process is extremely seamless. However, when things don't go according to plan, that's where you go. The Android Auto app has a hidden developer menu which exposes, amongst other things, video resolution options. To reach this menu, go to Settings on your phone, find Android Auto, go to Version Information, and tap it repeatedly to enable developer mode. This unlocks a three-dot menu under developer settings.

From there, scroll down the developer menu, tap Video Resolution, and set it to allow up to 1920x1080. Disconnect and reconnect Android Auto, and you'll see the difference immediately.

Navigation is where you notice it most

Street names and road markings become much easier to read

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Before we talk about just how big an improvement this is, it's worth noting that switching the resolution isn't some sharpening filter. Instead, it forces your Android phone to render the Android Auto stream at a higher resolution. If you're running a particularly old phone, that higher resolution could cause stutters. However, most modern phones should work particularly fine.

The biggest upgrade you'll see is during navigation. I spend a lot of time using Google Maps or alternatives like Organic Maps through Android Auto. While a lower-resolution stream is fine for basic navigation, a higher-resolution stream is essential for reading place names comfortably. Whether it's street names or road markings, a sharp interface makes it easier to read.

Navigation benefits from a sharper stream, but it's not the only use case. For example, I use Symfonium for my personal music library. When I have it up on Android Auto, a sharper screen makes browsing albums and playlists more comfortable. It also makes album art look better. The same extends to other media streaming apps like Pocket Casts for podcasts, or even Spotify if streaming music is more your thing.

Elsewhere, I don't do much messaging while driving, but if I do glance at the screen, the sharper text rendering is appreciated.

The best part of solving this problem is that the solution is one and done. Once you switch the output resolution, you don't need to change it every single time. It sticks. Similarly, you don't need to change any hardware or make any software investment. It's a simple solution to a simple problem.

One setting that fixes all resolution-related problems

I've never had a reason to dig through Android Auto's settings. However, with this resolution mismatch bothering me incessantly, I decided to do something I should've done sooner. In fact, it proved that sometimes it's worth looking beyond those standard settings.

Switching the display resolution settings was all it took for my phone to output a higher-resolution video to my Android Auto head unit. As a result, I get sharper visuals in Google Maps, Organic Maps, and Waze. Additionally, it makes text look sharper in everything from messaging apps to music streaming apps. If your Android Auto screen looks a bit blurrier than it should, this is the one setting I'd recommend checking.

Whether Maxis or Omni is the better fit will come down to the build and how much of the sensor-driven feature set is actually needed day-to-day, but both are worth a look for anyone interested in upgrading their chair.

item.title: I used this self-hosted tool to sort through my budget and it gave me more clarity than my banking app
item.itunes:title: I used this self-hosted tool to sort through my budget and it gave me more clarity than my banking app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Trying to manage my budget for the past few months has been difficult. No matter how careful I am about my spending, I reach the end of the month with much less left over in my bank account than expected. When I try to wrap my head around my income and expenses, my banking app is no help either. Its money tracking feature is underpowered and requires manual categorization of all my transactions, turning it into a time sink.

Meanwhile, third-party apps raise privacy concerns, leaving me stuck with my default banking app and its underpowered features. However, I recently came across Securo on GitHub, which allows you to analyze my transactions without sharing your data with a third party. So I decided to give the self-hosted service a try.

7 reasons Wallos is the best way to track your subscriptions

This open-source subscription tracking app is surprisingly powerful

2
By  Megan Ellis

What is Securo?

A self-hosted financial management

Securo is a self-hosted financial management app that lets you categorize your transactions, set up goals for yourself, and view reports on your spending.

The app allows you to import your bank statements onto your server, but you can also link the app directly with your bank using different providers. However, this involves more setup and may depend on your bank's own API usage terms.

Besides giving you an overview of your transactions, Securo lets you set up different rules to automatically categorize your income and expenses. It also allows you to set up savings goals, as well as a list of recurring transactions like subscriptions or bills. When setting up the service, you also have the ability to enable agents if you want an AI assistant to analyze your Securo data. However, I found that the tool already provided plenty of filters and graphs to help sort through your own data.

Getting started with Securo

Import and create rules for easy categorization

I chose to import my bank statements to Securo rather than linking my bank account, mostly because I wanted to see how the app performed without fiddling around with APIs. I'd recommend using an import if you first want to try out the app to see if it suits your needs.

The most difficult part is making sure that your uploaded document is compatible with Securo's import template. I spent a considerable amount of time fixing my bank's date formatting, which would not let me automatically convert it with my spreadsheet software because it was in a non-traditional format.

Next, there's categorizing your transactions. Rather than doing this one-by-one on the import screen, I recommend importing your transactions and then using rules to assign categories. You will also likely need to add new categories to fit your own lifestyle, which is luckily easy to do. For example, I split my income streams into different sources, and added expense categories like my phone contract and pet-related expenses.

Once you've set up your categories, you should set up some rules. Securo includes a few default rules you can use, but you can create your own. These can be applied to existing transactions so that you don't have to manually categorize all your data. For example, I used a rule to assign all transactions from my local grocery stores to the Groceries category. The rule creation window even allows you to preview a rule so that you can see how it will apply to the transactions you currently have on your account.

The initial setup takes some time, but once you have your rules in place, it gets a lot easier to import your data and get an immediate dashboard.

Securo's visual tools help sort through the data

Different visuals help you understand your spending

Securo gives you plenty of ways to sort through your data. In the Reports tab, you can see a variety of visual representations of your transactions including Net Worth, Income vs Expenses, Cash Flow, and Money Map.

I found the Money Map and Income vs Expenses tools particularly helpful, as they visualized my data in a way that made more sense to me. It helped me see that part of the reason I've been struggling with my budget is that my income is immediately taken up by my health and housing costs, leaving me with very little room for groceries and other expenses.

Applying filters to the Transactions tab also helped me get a better idea of what I was spending my money on. Ever the self-critic, I assumed I had simply been spending too much on food, takeout coffee, and my hobbies. But when I filtered for these over the past three months, the expenses were minimal and greatly reined in over the past few weeks.

These tools helped me identify the real problem — even though I had cut my expenses, my income had also reduced. This was down to periods of illness that meant I couldn't get as much work done. Meanwhile, while I was able to reduce spending on groceries, things like medication costs remained the same.

While the data doesn't sort my predicament, it did give me direction on where to steer my energy. I had been so focused on cutting costs and assuming that I had made many unnecessary transactions, when, in fact, it's a problem of income dips that make it more difficult to afford the essential costs.

I can now stop beating myself up and focus instead on trying to increase my work so that my income rises too. It's not easy when you're chronically ill, but I now know what to focus on.

I finally self-hosted my passwords, and it's simpler than I expected

I kept my passwords in the cloud for years, until Vaultwarden made self-hosting feel surprisingly simple.

1
By  Yash Patel

There are still some things I would like to see Securo add

Overall I had a really positive experience with Securo, to the point that I'm looking at whether I can set up a link to my bank account using an API. However, the app also has some room for improvement. Currently, the service doesn't support as many currencies as I would like, including the South African Rand. This means my dashboard is currently in US dollars instead of my actual local currency.

I also think the app could benefit from custom reports, or looking at trends for specific categories over time. The reports dashboard does show some category trends, but you can't select which ones you would like to see. Despite this, I think Securo is a really promising tool, and one of the most powerful self-hosted apps I've tried in a while.

Its money tracking feature is underpowered and requires manual categorization of all my transactions, turning it into a time sink.

Meanwhile, third-party apps raise privacy concerns, leaving me stuck with my default banking app and its underpowered features. However, I recently came across Securo on GitHub, which allows you to analyze my transactions without sharing your data with a third party. So I decided to give the self-hosted service a try.

What is Securo?

A self-hosted financial management

Securo is a self-hosted financial management app that lets you categorize your transactions, set up goals for yourself, and view reports on your spending.

The app allows you to import your bank statements onto your server, but you can also link the app directly with your bank using different providers. However, this involves more setup and may depend on your bank's own API usage terms.

Besides giving you an overview of your transactions, Securo lets you set up different rules to automatically categorize your income and expenses. It also allows you to set up savings goals, as well as a list of recurring transactions like subscriptions or bills. When setting up the service, you also have the ability to enable agents if you want an AI assistant to analyze your Securo data. However, I found that the tool already provided plenty of filters and graphs to help sort through your own data.

Getting started with Securo

Import and create rules for easy categorization

I chose to import my bank statements to Securo rather than linking my bank account, mostly because I wanted to see how the app performed without fiddling around with APIs. I'd recommend using an import if you first want to try out the app to see if it suits your needs.

The most difficult part is making sure that your uploaded document is compatible with Securo's import template. I spent a considerable amount of time fixing my bank's date formatting, which would not let me automatically convert it with my spreadsheet software because it was in a non-traditional format.

Next, there's categorizing your transactions. Rather than doing this one-by-one on the import screen, I recommend importing your transactions and then using rules to assign categories. You will also likely need to add new categories to fit your own lifestyle, which is luckily easy to do. For example, I split my income streams into different sources, and added expense categories like my phone contract and pet-related expenses.

Once you've set up your categories, you should set up some rules. Securo includes a few default rules you can use, but you can create your own. These can be applied to existing transactions so that you don't have to manually categorize all your data. For example, I used a rule to assign all transactions from my local grocery stores to the Groceries category. The rule creation window even allows you to preview a rule so that you can see how it will apply to the transactions you currently have on your account.

The initial setup takes some time, but once you have your rules in place, it gets a lot easier to import your data and get an immediate dashboard.

Securo's visual tools help sort through the data

Different visuals help you understand your spending

Securo gives you plenty of ways to sort through your data. In the Reports tab, you can see a variety of visual representations of your transactions including Net Worth, Income vs Expenses, Cash Flow, and Money Map.

I found the Money Map and Income vs Expenses tools particularly helpful, as they visualized my data in a way that made more sense to me. It helped me see that part of the reason I've been struggling with my budget is that my income is immediately taken up by my health and housing costs, leaving me with very little room for groceries and other expenses.

Applying filters to the Transactions tab also helped me get a better idea of what I was spending my money on. Ever the self-critic, I assumed I had simply been spending too much on food, takeout coffee, and my hobbies. But when I filtered for these over the past three months, the expenses were minimal and greatly reined in over the past few weeks.

These tools helped me identify the real problem — even though I had cut my expenses, my income had also reduced. This was down to periods of illness that meant I couldn't get as much work done. Meanwhile, while I was able to reduce spending on groceries, things like medication costs remained the same.

While the data doesn't sort my predicament, it did give me direction on where to steer my energy. I had been so focused on cutting costs and assuming that I had made many unnecessary transactions, when, in fact, it's a problem of income dips that make it more difficult to afford the essential costs.

I can now stop beating myself up and focus instead on trying to increase my work so that my income rises too. It's not easy when you're chronically ill, but I now know what to focus on.

I kept my passwords in the cloud for years, until Vaultwarden made self-hosting feel surprisingly simple.

There are still some things I would like to see Securo add

Overall I had a really positive experience with Securo, to the point that I'm looking at whether I can set up a link to my bank account using an API. However, the app also has some room for improvement. Currently, the service doesn't support as many currencies as I would like, including the South African Rand. This means my dashboard is currently in US dollars instead of my actual local currency.

I also think the app could benefit from custom reports, or looking at trends for specific categories over time. The reports dashboard does show some category trends, but you can't select which ones you would like to see. Despite this, I think Securo is a really promising tool, and one of the most powerful self-hosted apps I've tried in a while.
